To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we found mutations in 11 out of 14 cases of alleged vaccine encepahlopathy, and that these cases were all genetically determined epileptic encpahlapathies that arose de novo.

we identified SCN1A mutations in 11 of the 14 patients we studied who had been diagnosed with "vaccine encephalopathy." We found that all 9 cases in which parental DNA was available had de novo mutations in SCN1A.
de-novo mutations of SCN1A were present in 11/14 cases with alleged vaccine encepahalopathy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic causes of epilepsy and the implications for clinical practice.
the genetic and environmental causes of encephalopathies.
the identification and characterisation of genes and genetic variants that contribute to the development of epilepsy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of cases of alleged vaccine encepahlopathy in fact have a genetic cause and that vaccination is not a cause of the disorder.

de novo mutations in SCN1A may be the cause of a proportion of cases of alleged vaccine encepahopathy, and that the clinical presentation of the condition is that of an epileptic encephelopathy with a specific clinical phenotype, and is not vaccine encephalitis.
the alleged vaccine encephaly is in fact de novo mutations in the neuronal voltage gated sodium channel alpha1 gene (SCN 1A).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

de novo mutations of the neuronal sodium channel gene, SCN1A, are a common cause of alleged vaccine encepahlopathy, and that the clinical phenotype is that of severe myoclonus epilepsy of infancy (Dravet Syndrome).
de-novo mutations of SCN1A can cause an epilepsy syndrome that can be mistaken for vaccine encephalitis.
de-novo mutations of SCN1A can be identified in a high proportion of children with alleged vaccine encepahlopathy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified de novo mutations in the sodium channel gene (SCN)1A in patients with alleged vaccine-related encephalopathy, and that the seizures were not vaccine related.
the majority of cases of alleged vaccine encepalopathy are in fact genetic epilepsy disorders, and not vaccine-related.
we identified a genetic cause of vaccine encephalitis, and that it was not the vaccine, but rather the genetic cause.
